note: AUTHORED game catalogue. Species are real regional species named generally; every stat is an AUTHORED game number on a 1-5 scale (not a size, weight, limit or record); seasons are approximate game calendars; facts are general and name only the kind of source.

habitats.lake: open lake water with a shoreline

rods.title: Cane pole
rods.tip: No reel: swing the bait out and lift the fish straight up - simple and gentle for panfish.

rods.title: Spinning rod
rods.tip: An open-face reel that is easy to learn; the drag lets line slip before it breaks.

rods.title: Baitcasting rod
rods.tip: Accurate and strong, but a careless cast can tangle the spool (a 'backlash') - thumb the spool.

rods.title: Fly rod
rods.tip: The weight is in the line, not the lure: the rod loads the line and a light fly follows.

rods.title: Surf rod
rods.tip: A long rod to reach past near-shore water from a bank or beach.

rods.title: Crab line
rods.tip: A weighted line with bait and no hook: pull it in slowly and scoop the crab with a net.

rods.title: Crawfish trap
rods.tip: A mesh trap with funnel entrances: set it, wait, then run the trap line and check each one.

species.title: Largemouth bass
species.fact: Its upper jaw reaches back past the eye - the easiest way to tell it from other black basses.
species.handling: Wet your hands, support its body level and keep it in the water while you unhook it.

species.title: Bluegill
species.fact: Bluegill are sunfish that nest in shallow colonies, and the males guard the nests.
species.handling: Smooth the sharp top fin down from front to back before you hold it.

species.title: Redear sunfish
species.fact: Redear sunfish eat snails, which is why many anglers call them shellcrackers.
species.handling: Use a small hook and a dehooker so the fish goes back quickly.

species.title: Crappie
species.fact: Crappie often school around sunken brush and other cover, so where you find one you may find more.
species.handling: Their mouths tear easily: reel steadily and lift gently.

species.title: Channel catfish
species.fact: Catfish find much of their food by taste and smell - their whisker-like barbels carry taste buds.
species.handling: Hold it behind the side and top spines; those spines can give a painful jab.

species.title: Red drum (redfish)
species.fact: Red drum usually carry one or more dark spots near the tail.
species.handling: Support its weight with two hands and let it swim off on its own before you let go.

species.title: Spotted seatrout
species.fact: Spotted seatrout carry scattered black spots on the back, fins and tail.
species.handling: Keep it in the water and handle it as little as possible - its slime coat protects it.

species.title: Southern flounder
species.fact: Flounder are flatfish: as they grow, both eyes move to one side of the head so they can lie flat and ambush prey.
species.handling: Lay it flat on a wet hand and slide it back into the water.

species.title: Blue crab
species.fact: Blue crabs are swimming crabs: their last pair of legs is flattened like paddles.
species.handling: Hold a crab from behind, at the back legs, away from the claws; rules often protect egg-bearing females - return them.

species.title: Red swamp crawfish
species.fact: Red swamp crawfish dig burrows and wait out dry months underground until water returns.
species.handling: Keep a catch cool, damp and shaded; release small or egg-bearing crawfish where you found them.

species.title: Striped bass
species.fact: Striped bass move between salt and fresh water: many swim upriver to spawn.
species.handling: Keep your fingers out of the gills; hold it by the lower lip and support the belly.

species.title: California halibut
species.fact: Like every flatfish, a young halibut swims upright; one eye then migrates so the fish can lie flat on the sand.
species.handling: Its teeth are sharp: use pliers and keep the fish flat and wet.

species.title: Surfperch
species.fact: Surfperch give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
species.handling: Wet your hands and return it quickly - especially in spring, when females may be carrying young.

species.title: Dungeness crab
species.fact: Dungeness crabs often bury themselves in sandy bottoms with only their eyes showing.
species.handling: Hold from behind at the back legs; rules on size and sex apply to real crabbing - check the state wildlife agency.

species.title: Rainbow trout
species.fact: Rainbow trout need cool, oxygen-rich water, so they hold where currents mix and shade the stream.
species.handling: Barbless hooks and wet hands help a trout recover; keep it in the water for the photo.

species.title: Cutthroat trout
species.fact: Cutthroat trout are named for the red-orange slash under the lower jaw.
species.handling: Face it into gentle current until it swims away strongly.

species.title: Brown trout
species.fact: Brown trout were brought to North America from Europe and are among the warier trout.
species.handling: Keep the fight short so the fish is not exhausted before release.

species.title: Smallmouth bass
species.fact: Smallmouth bass favour clearer, rockier water with some current.
species.handling: Hold by the lower lip with the body supported, then let it swim from your hand.

species.title: Yellow perch
species.fact: Yellow perch have dark vertical bars on a golden body and often travel in schools.
species.handling: Flatten the spiny top fin before gripping it.

honesty.play: Every catch, trap haul and codex entry is PLAY: stored only on this device, never a completion record, never money, never a licence.
honesty.real: Real activity follows state rules - check the state wildlife agency (Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries; California Department of Fish and Wildlife) for licences, seasons, sizes and limits.
honesty.seasons: Seasons here are approximate, game calendar - not the legal seasons.
honesty.facts: Species facts are general, from the kind of material state wildlife agencies publish in species profiles; game stats are AUTHORED on a 1-5 scale and are not sizes or records.
honesty.wildlife: Never approach, feed or harass wildlife; alligators share Gulf waters and are dangerous - keep your distance.
honesty.places: Fishing spots sit on AUTHORED water (procedural lakes, bayous, canals, ponds and terrain) - not the real waters.
